one_liner: Maintained C rewrite of nanomsg (Scalability Protocols). It beats nanomsg's pub/sub throughput only for very large messages.
what_it_does: NNG is a brokerless messaging library that implements the Scalability Protocols (PUB/SUB, REQ/REP, PUSH/PULL, BUS, PAIR, SURVEY) over inproc, IPC, TCP, TLS, WebSocket and UDP transports. It is wire-compatible with nanomsg and mangos peers. Its native API is different: nng_socket struct handles, dialers and listeners, nng_msg, asynchronous nng_aio operations, and per-socket contexts. NNG 1.x also ships an nn_* compatibility API; the 2.0 branch removes it.
how_it_is_fast: NNG replaces nanomsg's design, where each socket ran on a single worker thread driven by state machines, with an asynchronous I/O framework (nng_aio). Completion callbacks run on a task-thread pool, and platform pollers (epoll, kqueue, event ports) do the I/O. Contexts let one socket run many concurrent state machines. The PUB fan-out does not copy the message: it bumps a refcount per pipe and uses a small bounded queue per pipe. The TCP/IPC transports send an 8-byte length, the header and the body as one scatter-gather write, and on receive they allocate an exact-size message and read the body straight into it. Neither the paper nor the project says which of these mechanisms produces the large-payload win over nanomsg.
when_to_use: Single-host PUB/SUB with very large messages: 256-512 KB over IPC, or above ~128 KB over TCP loopback. At these sizes NNG kept scaling toward ~2 GB/s, while nanomsg peaked around 1.5 GB/s and then declined.
Replacing unmaintained libnanomsg in an existing deployment. NNG talks the same wire protocol to nanomsg and mangos peers, and NNG 1.x can serve many nn_* callers through its compatibility layer.

Servers with many sockets, many peers or many in-flight requests. Contexts plus nng_aio let one REQ/REP socket serve many concurrent transactions without raw sockets, and the README says NNG's design gains most in exactly these cases.
Deployments that need TLS (Mbed TLS, wolfSSL or OpenSSL) or WebSocket transports, or that must build on Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD and illumos from one C codebase.
when_not_to_use: Small or medium messages where latency matters. In the SRDS 2025 study, nanomsg had the best average latency (IPC up to 128 KB) and ZeroMQ the best worst-case latency. NNG's jitter was higher: under ~10 us on average, with spikes at 512 KB.
Maximum raw throughput. The same study found ZeroMQ fastest across most transports and configurations (~2.9 GB/s peaks), and nanomsg the most CPU- and memory-efficient.
Simple single-threaded, synchronous applications. The README itself says legacy nanomsg may perform better there.
Code that relies on nanomsg's send/receive priorities (NN_SNDPRIO/NN_RCVPRIO), NN_LINGER or its statistics semantics. NNG does not support these, or supports them differently.
Lossless pub/sub, or cutting bandwidth with publisher-side filtering. PUB sends every message to every subscriber, subscribers filter locally, and both sides drop messages when their queues fill.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake build)
integration.dependencies: none for the core; optional Mbed TLS, wolfSSL or OpenSSL for TLS; CMake 3.15+ to build (Ninja recommended)
integration.min_toolchain: C11 compiler per the README (CMakeLists sets CMAKE_C_STANDARD 99); CMake 3.15+
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD, illumos/Solaris, Android, iOS; IPC uses UNIX domain sockets on POSIX and named pipes on Windows
integration.thread_safety: The 2.0 manual has no blanket statement. Sockets are ID handles resolved through a locked, refcounted table (issue #1724), so calls from multiple threads are supported. nng_aio callbacks may run on other NNG threads and need their own synchronization, and blocking NNG calls from NNG threads are documented as safe.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: wire-compatible with nanomsg and mangos peers. NNG 1.x ships an nn_* compat API (NNG_ENABLE_COMPAT, on by default) that lacks NN_SNDPRIO, NN_RCVPRIO, NN_IPV4ONLY and the stats API. NNG 2.0 removes the compat API and requires porting to nng_* calls plus an explicit nng_init().

gotchas: Pub/sub is lossy by default, and the loss is silent. Each subscriber pipe on the PUB side has a 16-message send queue (NNG_OPT_SENDBUF, counted in messages, not bytes) that drops the oldest message when full. On the SUB side, NNG_OPT_SUB_PREFNEW=true discards older unreceived messages. Watch the tx_discard stats.
The main branch is 2.0 development (2.0.0-beta.2, Aug 2026) with breaking API changes and no libnanomsg compat layer. The README points production users to the stable branch (1.12.x).

Security: GHSA-8rrv-25fw-rm86 (integer overflow in nni_msg_alloc) lets a remote peer abort the process with one crafted length header; it is fixed in 1.12.3 and 2.0.0-alpha.7. Set NNG_OPT_RECVMAXSZ for untrusted peers (the 2.0 docs give the default as 1 GiB; 0 means unlimited). The HTTP directory-handler path traversal (GHSA-rv5j-2q4p-qm56) is fixed only in the v1.12.4 tag.
No default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE is set. A plain 'cmake -G Ninja ..' build, which is what the benchmark suite used for NNG 1.9.0, is likely unoptimized, so pass -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick NNG over NanoMsg when you need an actively maintained, wire-compatible library, TLS/WebSocket, multi-threaded concurrency via contexts, or large-payload throughput; stay on NanoMsg for small-message latency and CPU efficiency. Pick it over shared-memory or single-host specialists such as msgq or TCPSHM when you need portable network transports and the full set of SP patterns rather than the lowest same-host latency.
verified_claims_summary: An independent Hitachi Energy study (IEEE SRDS 2025, arXiv 2508.07934) benchmarked PUB/SUB on one Xeon w3-2435 host (8 cores, 64 GB). It compared NNG 1.9.0 (built from source with CMake and no build type) against distro-packaged libnanomsg 1.1.5 and libzmq 4.3.4, using 1-512 KB messages over inproc, IPC and TCP loopback. NNG out-threw nanomsg only at the two largest IPC sizes, and above ~128 KB on TCP, where it reached ~2 GB/s against nanomsg's ~1.5 GB/s peak. ZeroMQ led overall at ~2.9 GB/s. The paper gives no compiler flags; the C harness is built with gcc -O2.
